# The interplay of lipid droplets, mitochondria, and ER in governing hepatic lipid metabolism

**Authors:** William A. Hofstadter; Mari V. Reid; Douglas G. Mashek

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Biochemistry, Molecular Biology and Biophysics, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, USA | 2Department of Medicine, Division of Diabetes, Endocrinology, and Metabolism, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, USA | 3Masonic Institute on the Biology of Aging and Metabolism, University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Minneapolis, MN, USA

## Introduction

Lipid metabolism and storage are highly compartmentalized processes. Key organelles defined to govern lipid synthesis (ER), storage (lipid droplets, LDs), and catabolism (mitochondria) work in synchrony to coordinate lipid metabolic flux. Interactions between these organelles play important roles in metabolite exchange and signaling that vary in response to physiological conditions. Alterations in organelle crosstalk or imbalances between anabolic and catabolic pathways are commonly observed in diseased states, including metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). While many studies have characterized two-organelle interactions (e.g., LD-mitochondria), there is a general lack of consideration of how the presence of other organelles impacts the function of these contacts. This review aims to provide a concise summary of the regulation, function, and complexity of these organelle interactions that compartmentalize hepatic lipid metabolism.

## Organelle interactions that contribute to lipid catabolism

To parse apart the function of LD-mitochondria contacts, mitochondria are commonly classified as interacting with LDs, termed peridroplet mitochondria (PDM), or those distant to LDs - cytoplasmic mitochondria (CM). Importantly, mitochondria are not static as peridroplet or cytoplasmic sub-populations, but rather their propensity for LD interactions is regulated by the metabolic needs of the cell. Indeed, while most LD-mitochondria last only a few seconds, contacts can be stabilized to persist for several minutes [1]. Several studies in adipocytes and hepatocytes have provided evidence that CM specialize in catabolism, exhibiting enhanced capacity for oxidative respiration and fatty acid (FA) oxidation, while PDM facilitate de novo lipogenesis and FA esterification [2,3]. Accordingly, a flux of FAs towards CM and away from PDM is observed following starvation, a catabolic stimulus [3]. However, recent reports suggest that CM are not devoid of LDs but instead interact with many smaller LDs [4]. These authors found that diabetic models exhibited an increased number of small LDs in contact with CM, a phenomenon that correlated with increased FA oxidation and respiration [4]. In a separate study, it was found that hepatocytes of mice fed a high-fat diet had mitochondria that interacted with larger LDs [5]. However, if the mice exercised, mitochondria interacted with smaller LDs and exhibited enhanced respiration and FA oxidation [5]. These findings are consistent with those in white adipose tissue (WAT), demonstrating that mitochondria bound to smaller LDs exhibit enhanced respiration [6]. Mitochondrial elongation is also important for their ability to engage with LDs and promote FA oxidation [5,7]. These findings suggest that an additional layer of regulation exists to tune the function of LD-mitochondria contacts based on organelle morphology.

Further evidence of the direct cooperation between LDs and mitochondria for lipid catabolism comes from the analysis of LD-mitochondria membrane contact site (MCS) proteins, which commonly mediate organelle tethering to promote the exchange of biomolecules [8]. For example, the SNARE protein SNAP23 has been proposed to facilitate FA transfer at LD-mitochondria MCSs. While SNAP23 localizes to several different compartments, upon fasting SNAP23 is recruited to LDs via the LD-resident Perilipin 2 (PLIN2), where it interacts with mitochondrial ACSL1 [9–11]. SNAP23 is well situated to regulate FA oxidation via this interaction, as mitochondria-localized ACSL1 enhances FA oxidation [12]. Indeed, loss of SNAP23 is associated with dampened FA oxidation and decreased PLIN2 abundance in the mitochondria fraction, suggesting decreased LD-mitochondria contacts [13]. Another key LD-mitochondria MCS protein is Perilipin 5 (PLIN5), which has been shown to promote LD-mitochondria tethering and enhance FA incorporation into TGs [14]. Despite its established anabolic role, PLIN5 inhibition decreases FA oxidation [15], specifically within the CM population [3]. AMPK signaling, which activates catabolic processes under fasting conditions, was found to promote interactions between Rab8a and PLIN5 to induce LD-mitochondria contacts and FA oxidation [16]. While a three-amino acid truncation is sufficient to prevent LD tethering to mitochondria, this mutant shows minimal disruptions to both catabolic and anabolic lipid metabolism [17]. This result highlights that PDM formation is dispensable for FA oxidation and that interaction with the ER (which is likely maintained with this mutant) may be the critical factor necessary to maintain normal FA esterification. Similarly to PLIN5, knockout of the LD-mitochondria MCS protein MFN2 also suppresses FA oxidation in CM specifically [5]. It is important to note that both PLIN5 and MFN2 have well-described functions independent of LD-mitochondria contacts that could contribute to these effects [18–20]. These LD-mitochondria MCS proteins can have several roles in regulating FA oxidation, from physically tethering organelles together to directly transferring lipids between membranes. While proteins such as MFN2 are thought to catalyze the former, the lipid transfer protein VPS13D has been found to facilitate the latter [21]. VPS13 proteins localize to LD-mitochondria contacts and bind FAs [22]. Accordingly, loss of VPS13D is associated with decreased lipid transfer from LDs to mitochondria and suppressed FA oxidation [21].

While LDs and mitochondria are the main drivers of lipid catabolism, accumulating evidence suggests coordination with other organelles may contribute to this function. For example, the chemical disruption of ER-mitochondria contacts was found to dampen CM FA oxidation [3]. Furthermore, a tripartite complex promoting LD-mitochondria-ER contacts was discovered, the disruption of which dampens FA oxidation [23]. While in steady-state, this multi-organelle contact has been observed to persist for minutes [1], the abundance and extent of contact can be further enhanced through both fasting and treatment with oleic acid, suggesting that this is a multifunctional interaction [3]. It is important to consider that the FA substrate needed for oxidation could be obtained from many different organelles, not just LDs. VPS13 proteins localize to several different MCSs in addition to LD-mitochondria, suggesting that they could regulate FA oxidation through lipid transfer between ER, mitochondrial, LD, endosomal, and peroxisomal membranes [22,24]. Similarly, FA oxidation does not always occur in the mitochondria. In response to the disruption of LD-mitochondria contacts through PLIN5 knockdown, several peroxisomal pathways were found to be upregulated at LD-associated ER-mitochondria contacts, including a potentially compensatory increase in peroxisomal FA oxidation [3]. Altogether, these findings show how lipid catabolism can be tuned by the induction of diverse organelle contacts that ultimately facilitate the transfer of FAs into mitochondria and peroxisomes.

## Organelle interactions that promote lipid anabolism

Historically, the general dogma has been that the interactions between LDs and mitochondria exist exclusively to support catabolic lipid metabolism. However, an expanding body of evidence highlights the important role of the ER in forming a tripartite interaction that facilitates anabolic lipid metabolism and LD expansion. The earliest characterization of anabolic lipid metabolism in PDM was found in brown adipose tissue (BAT). Benador et al. found that PDM have a reduced capacity for FA oxidation, but have increased flux through the TCA cycle and greater respiratory capacity to support TAG synthesis. Furthermore, they demonstrated that the ability of PLIN5 overexpression to increase TAG levels is dependent on its ability to tether the LD and mitochondria via its C-terminal region [2]. Since this initial publication, a series of papers have supported the idea that PDM coordinates lipogenesis, whereas CM prioritizes lipid catabolism. This phenomenon has been observed in a variety of tissue types, including the liver [3,4,25–27]. These contacts are also zonated across the liver, with periportal hepatocytes having larger LDs and more PDM than pericentral hepatocytes [27].

PLIN5 has been identified as the most critical tether in PDM formation, and a key regulator of lipid metabolism. Overexpression of PLIN5 drives PDM formation, and this tethering is dependent on the C-terminal domain of the protein [17,27,28]. While some have removed the whole C-terminal domain [27,28], removal of the last three amino acids is sufficient to prevent LD and mitochondrial tethering [17]. The phosphorylation of PLIN5 by PKA during fasting is a critical modification that facilitates the switch from anabolic to catabolic metabolism. Upon phosphorylation at S155, PLIN5 leaves the LD and is translocated to the nucleus, where it promotes the transcription of genes involved in oxidative metabolism [20,29]. This phosphorylation also impacts organelle interactions. It was recently demonstrated in mouse livers that the expression of a phosphomimetic PLIN5 reduces LD and mitochondrial contact, even when the mice are fed a western diet [27]. These livers contain fewer and smaller LDs and more free fatty acids in the serum, suggestive of more lipolytic activity. On the other hand, expressing a phosphodead PLIN5 increases PDM formation, LD expansion, and TAG accumulation in the liver [27]. Other papers have suggested that the phosphomimetic mutant increases FA oxidation by promoting PDM formation [28], however, these studies did not measure oxidation in PDM specifically nor interrogate the transcriptional contribution of PLIN5. These studies also show that PLIN5 interacts with FATP4, which was posited to be a mitochondrial protein [28]. However, FATP4 is an established ER protein [30–33], suggesting this interaction may be more complex than initially anticipated. Regardless, these findings highlight the role of the ER at PDM, which is critical for supporting anabolic metabolism at these sites.

The ER in proximity to mitochondria are commonly referred to as mitochondria-associated membranes (MAMs). MAMs are well characterized and are known to spatially regulate mitochondrial calcium homeostasis, mitochondrial dynamics, and nutrient trafficking (reviewed in [34–36]). Nearly every interaction between mitochondria and LDs also features the presence of the ER wrapping around and/or between the other two organelles [3]. This three-way interaction is known as PDM-MAM. Despite this, most papers comparing the metabolic activity of PDM and CM characterize mitochondria and LDs, while neglecting the ER. Recognizing the tripartite nature of these interactions is critical, as the majority of enzymes involved in de novo lipogenesis (DNL) and FA esterification reside in the ER, along with other important signaling proteins that help coordinate mitochondrial activity [34]. While DNL enzymes are primarily found in the ER, recent work has shown that the synthesis of phosphoenolpyruvate, used to generate the glycerol backbone for glycerolipid synthesis, occurs in the mitochondria in lipogenic cells, including the liver [37]. These findings highlight the contribution of all three organelles to lipogenesis and fatty acid esterification. In the liver, MAMs specific to CM and PDM have unique proteomes that are geared to support their associated mitochondria’s metabolic function. CM-MAM is enriched in proteins involved in protein translation and ER organization, while PDM-MAM is enriched for proteins involved in lipid anabolic pathways [3]. Exactly how these proteins become compartmentalized at these two distinct MAMs remains unknown. What is clear is that intact MAM is essential for maintaining both CM and PDM metabolic function. Disrupting the flow of calcium from the ER to mitochondria decreases FA oxidation in CM, and uncoupling MAMs reduces the ability of PDM to esterify FAs [3].

Studies are beginning to elucidate what proteins help establish these three-way contact sites to support DNL and FA esterification. In WAT, the mitochondrial protein mitogaurdin 2 (MIGA2) has been identified as a key PDM-MAM tether. MIGA2 simultaneously binds the LD through an LD binding domain and the ER through its FFAT motif that is recognized by VAP-A/VAP-B [38]. MIGA2 expression is sufficient to induce PDM formation and TAG production and is necessary for LD expansion during adipocyte differentiation [38]. In Huh7 hepatocytes, the ER resident proteins oxysterol-binding protein-related protein 5 (ORP5) and ORP8 are recruited to sites of LD budding and expansion. These proteins were previously identified as transporters of phosphatidylserine at MAMs but have been recently implicated in promoting LD expansion at PDM-MAM contact sites. In response to lipid loading, ORP5/8 are recruited to MAMs through interactions with phosphatidic acid-enriched domains in the ER [39] and the mitochondrial tether protein tyrosine phosphatase-interacting protein 51 (PTPIP51) [40]. ORP5/8 then recruits Seipin to these contact sites, which facilitates the budding and release of LDs from the ER. The loss of ORP5/8 or PTPIP51 decreases LD numbers [39]. These examples each demonstrate how important forming and maintaining PDM-MAM are for supporting organelle interactions and facilitating lipid storage in a variety of cell types.

## Lipid compartmentalization and disease

Disruptions in PDM and MAMs are common in a wide range of diseases (reviewed in [41–44]). In the context of MASLD, PDM accumulate in parallel with LDs in the early stages of steatosis, but there is nearly a complete loss of PDM with progression to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic hepatitis (MASH), which also coincides with reduced LDs at this advanced stage of liver disease [4,25,26,45]. In addition to simply having less PDM in MASH, the proteomic differences between PDM and CM are lost at this stage, which may contribute to metabolic inflexibility [26]. MAMs are also dysregulated in MAFLD, although both up- and downregulation of contact have been observed in the steatotic liver (reviewed in [46]).

The upregulation of PDM formation and LD accumulation at first may appear as pathogenic, but is increasingly recognized as a protective response to excess nutrient availability. LDs can sequester oxidized PUFAs and peroxidized lipid species to limit oxidative stress and prevent ferroptosis [47,48]. The chronic accumulation of saturated lipids in the ER induces the unfolded protein response during fatty liver [49,50]. As a response to the ER stress, lipolysis is upregulated to release monounsaturated oleate to increase membrane fluidity and promote the re-esterification of the toxic saturated FAs [51]. This process is likely facilitated through the differential metabolism of the PDM and CM. When comparing the morphology of PDM and CM between healthy and diseased livers, CM become significantly more fragmented with liver disease while PDM morphology remains largely unchanged [52]. These data suggest that PDM may be metabolically more resistant in a disease state, and upregulating their formation helps the cell respond to nutrient overload and remain metabolically flexible in the early stages of MASLD. However, more work is needed to better understand how PDM-MAM contributes to or limits MASLD and its progression to MASH.

## Summary and Future Directions

Despite recent progress, much remains to be determined regarding how hepatic lipid metabolism is compartmentalized within cells. For example, there are many conflicting reports in the literature about whether LD-mitochondria interactions facilitate catabolic or anabolic reactions. This may be due, in part, to the fact that very few studies directly measure the flow of FAs between LDs and mitochondria subpopulations. Indeed, many studies correlate an increase in mitochondria-LD overlap with increased FA oxidation and assume that the FA flux occurs through PDM. Experiments employing live cell imaging of organelle contacts simultaneous with organellar biosensors are needed to characterize the dynamics of these interactions, which are missed by measures in fixed cells or isolated organelles. Another potential source of these discrepancies is the grouping or assigning of organelle contacts to a specific function. However, a myriad of different proteins may facilitate these interactions to coordinate diverse, or even opposing, functions. As such, analyzing the proteomic and lipidomic composition of a given contact may help explain seemingly conflicting reports. Furthermore, putting these findings into the broader context of the cellular environment (nutrient availability, spatial localization within a tissue, presence of additional organelles, etc.) will help to mechanistically define what supports the formation of distinct organelle contacts in governing lipid metabolism. Ultimately, defining the uniqueness of these organelle contacts will likely open up therapeutic avenues targeting specific protein-protein interactions to mitigate disease development or progression.
